We introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 annotated recordings of heart sound abnormalities, sourced from the public Kaggle Heart Sound Recognition competition. The dataset encompasses six distinct conditions: Aortic Stenosis, Mitral Regurgitation, Mitral Stenosis, Normal, Pulmonary Stenosis, and Tricuspid Regurgitation. Our model integrates both attention and self-attention layers to automatically identify the most relevant segments for diagnosis. The proposed architecture, built upon a 1-D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), incorporates time attention, self-attention, and time-frequency attention modules. These components enable the network to independently select critical information for classification. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves a high average accuracy of 94.1% across all classes. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the model's performance across different classes and offer insights into the significance of specific signal segments. The source code and dataset are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmed-elsaid/Heart-Sound-Attention. This research underscores the potential of attention mechanisms in enhancing the accuracy of heart sound classification. Furthermore, the model's superior performance and lightweight architecture suggest its applicability to other heart sound classification tasks. Finally, the model's ability to highlight significant signal segments aids in understanding the diagnostic process and offers a pathway for explainable AI in heart sound classification. This concept is a cornerstone of computer science, as computable functions represent the most straightforward model of computation. This paper demonstrates that computable functions are precisely those that are Turing computable, thereby establishing the equivalence between Turing machines and Turing's original formulation of computability. The discussion begins by defining computable functions and outlining their fundamental properties. It then proceeds to prove the equivalence between Turing computable functions and Turing's original definition, followed by an examination of key characteristics of these functions. Finally, the paper addresses the issue of function complexity, specifically how the computational resources required vary with input size. This topic is particularly significant for computer scientists, as it elucidates the relationship between Turing machines and modern computers. By measuring the complex permittivity of sapphire across the 4–12 GHz frequency range using an open-ended coaxial probe, we determined the bulk dielectric loss tangent to be approximately $10^{-6}$ for sapphire oriented with its c-axis perpendicular to the measurement direction. of light traversing it, a phenomenon known as the Fizeau-Frenkel effect. This paper examines the conditions under which momentum is transferred between light and the medium. We demonstrate that, contrary to the classical Fizeau-Frenkel effect, these conditions are never fully met. Specifically, in the presence of magnetization, the optical path is defined only up to an arbitrary constant. Furthermore, the optical path exhibits dependence on the direction of light propagation, a finding that conflicts with the principle of time-reversal symmetry. These results are derived from a rigorous analysis of Maxwell's equations, utilizing the constitutive relations for a dielectric medium with magnetization. The study also explores the implications of these findings for the energy conservation law. Ultimately, the analysis reveals that the classical description of the Fizeau-Frenkel effect is incomplete. Additionally, we establish that the optical path is not equivalent to the phase accumulated by light within the medium. Finally, we show that the optical path differs from the phase of light in an isotropic medium with a refractive index given by the absolute value of the refractive index tensor determinant. These conclusions are applicable to any moving dielectric medium possessing magnetization. The paper concludes with a discussion of these outcomes. Keywords: Fizeau-Frenkel effect, optical path, moving dielectric medium, magnetization, time-reversal symmetry, energy conservation law. This study introduces a new noise-robust method for modeling the evolution of socioeconomic status using point process theory. Our findings indicate that the distribution of socioeconomic status in Brazil is skewed toward lower levels, a trend that has intensified over time. In this context, the deterministic and randomized (with error $\delta$) communication complexities are denoted as $D_n$ and $R_{\delta,n}$, respectively. We demonstrate that for any $\delta > 0$, the gap between $R_{\delta,n}$ and $D_n$ is at least $n^{\Omega(\delta)}$. This finding indicates that randomization offers only a limited advantage in solving set disjointness when disjointness is promised. This result also establishes a lower bound for the randomized communication complexity of the disjointness promise problem on intersection-closed families of sets. Furthermore, it complements recent findings by Hirahara, who showed that $R_{\delta,n}$ is at most $n^{O(\delta)}$. Additionally, our result implies that the quantum communication complexity of set disjointness with a disjointness promise is at most $n^{\Omega(\delta)}$, thereby resolving an open question posed by Yufei Jing. Finally, we extend our result to the case where $n$ players each hold a subset of $[m]$ (with $m \geq n$), yielding a lower bound of $m^{1/2 - \Omega(\delta)}$. Consequently, our result is nearly tight for the quantum setting. By employing spin-wave theory, we derive an analytical expression for $\chi(q)$ that aligns with Monte Carlo simulation results. This form elucidates the momentum structure of antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations, offering a basis for interpreting neutron scattering experiments on three-dimensional $S=1/2$ quantum antiferromagnets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the peak in $\chi(q)$ at the $(\pi,\pi,\pi)$ wave vector is significantly broader than in classical antiferromagnets, indicating that quantum fluctuations substantially weaken the antiferromagnetic order. Finally, we show that the momentum dependence of $\chi(q)$ near the wave vector $\boldsymbol{Q}=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$ is governed by a single parameter, the spin-wave renormalization factor $Z$, which can be determined from the zero-momentum limit $\chi(0)$. bb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is defined as a meromorphic self-map of the Riemann sphere. The postcritical set of such a map, denoted $Pc(f)$, consists of the forward orbit of its critical points. This study investigates the topological characteristics of $Pc(f)$ within the space $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$. Specifically, it establishes a criterion for a compact subset $K\subset\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ to be realized as $Pc(f)$ for some rational map $f$. The paper demonstrates that if $K$ is both locally connected and simply connected, it can be the postcritical set of a rational map. Furthermore, it proves that if $K$ is the postcritical set of a rational map $f$, then $K$ is locally connected if and only if $Pc(f)$ is locally connected. Finally, the study examines the relationship between the local connectivity of $Pc(f)$ and the dynamics of $f$ on its Fatou set. It is shown that if $Pc(f)$ is locally connected, then $f$ is either conjugate to a rational function possessing only multiple Fatou components or is post-critically finite. Additionally, it is proven that if $Pc(f)$ is locally connected, then $Pc(f^{\circ n})$ is also locally connected for all $n\geq 1$. These findings extend and complement the work of R. Douady and J. This result was previously conjectured by Ono and Soundararajan for $p=2$ and subsequently generalized by Bergé for all $p$. Our approach relies on Bergé's method, which employs Bergman's inequality to derive a lower bound for specific determinants of the Fourier coefficients. Our computational findings suggest that this broader conjecture holds true for $p < 1000$. Although SC approaches have been extensively utilized in economics and political science, their application within the medical field remains limited. This study introduces a novel SC framework designed to address time-to-event outcomes. The proposed method constructs a weighted combination of control units to emulate the treated unit's trajectory, with weights derived from a kernel function that integrates both time and event-free survival information. This paper investigates semi-clusters, which are defined as disjoint unions of semi-transitive graphs that possess identical numbers of non-transitive 2-paths and 3-paths. We demonstrate that every semi-transitive graph can be constructed from cycles through an operation involving the subdivision of an even cycle and the addition of a chord. Furthermore, we establish that the class of semi-transitive graphs is closed under taking induced subgraphs and that every finite semi-transitive graph admits a specific structural decomposition. These findings yield an infinite hierarchy of semi-transitive classes and facilitate the enumeration of non-isomorphic semi-transitive graphs up to a given size. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm for recognizing semi-transitive graphs. The results also extend to a broader category of graphs known as semi-transitive-like graphs, a subclass of strongly chordal graphs that encompasses both semi-transitive graphs and strongly mixed graphs. Consequently, our findings contribute to the ongoing effort to characterize strongly mixed graphs. Finally, we present a family of strongly mixed graphs that cannot be formed by combining odd and even cycles, thereby addressing an open question posed by Hellwig and Neumann. This family consists of strongly mixed graphs that are not semi-transitive and lack a non-transitive 3-path, a group that remains infinite even when restricted to graphs with a bounded number of vertices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the maximum clique size of a strongly mixed graph can be determined in polynomial time. These outcomes are significant because they offer a novel approach to the longstanding problem of recognizing strongly mixed graphs, a task that is otherwise known to be NP-hard. Finally, we offer a new characterization of strongly mixed graphs, thereby advancing the understanding of this graph class. Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will detect thousands of gravitational wave (GW) host galaxies, yet their redshifts will remain unknown. To address this, we propose a novel method for estimating host galaxy redshifts by training a machine learning model on the correlation between GW source properties and host galaxy properties. We demonstrate that this approach can achieve a median redshift estimation accuracy of $\Delta z \sim 0.005$ for GW190521-like events and $\Delta z \sim 0.002$ for GW191210-like events. This accuracy is sufficient to determine the Hubble constant ($H_0$) to a precision of $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 1.5$ km/s/Mpc using just 100 GW events. We show that these results can be further improved by incorporating additional data from the Euclid mission. Our findings indicate that a combination of Euclid and LSST observations could constrain $H_0$ to a precision of $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 0.5$ km/s/Mpc. This represents a significant advancement for the standard siren method, bringing it closer to its full potential. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these measurements can effectively break the current $H_0$ tension. Our study also highlights the critical role of machine learning in advancing gravitational wave astronomy. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for cosmology and the standard siren technique. Our code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekgupta1234/ML_for_H0}. This study examines the production of these lepton pairs in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 200$ GeV using data from the PHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). The observed $p_{\rm T}$ distributions align well with predictions derived from a photon-photon fusion model, which incorporates initial state radiation and final state lepton energy loss within the medium. Furthermore, the ratio of lepton pair yields in central to peripheral collisions matches predictions that account for photon-photon fusion occurring both inside and outside the hot dense medium. These findings provide robust evidence for lepton pair production via photon-photon fusion in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 200$ GeV. The results also support the substantial contribution of medium lepton pairs to the total yield in the low $p_{\rm T}$ region, offering a novel method to investigate the properties of the hot dense matter. Finally, the data constrain the photon virtuality and the energy loss of final state leptons within the medium. These measurements are crucial for understanding the properties of the hot dense matter and for the search for the Higgs boson at RHIC. with identity) is defined as a collection of subrings whose union equals $R$. The covering number $\omega(R)$ represents the minimum cardinality of such a cover. A cover consisting of proper subgroups of a group $G$ is termed minimal if the removal of any single subgroup results in a cover that is no longer minimal. This paper investigates minimal covers of minimal $p$-groups. Specifically, for a minimal $p$-group $G$, we establish that $\omega(G) \leq \frac{p+1}{2} + 1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $G$ is minimally covered by $n$ subgroups of order $p^k$, then $k \leq \log_p\left(\frac{p^{n-1}-1}{p-1}\right) + 1$. Finally, we characterize minimal covers of abelian $p$-groups and provide a complete classification of minimal covers for minimally generated $p$-groups where $p \leq 3$. Additionally, we construct an infinite family of non-abelian $p$-groups that possess minimal covers of arbitrary size. These findings extend and refine several recent results by the authors and other researchers. Notably, our work corrects and improves a claim by R. R. R. Sharma and S. K. Rana, who asserted that for a minimally generated $p$-group $G$, $\omega(G) \leq \frac{p+1}{2} + 1$. We demonstrate that this assertion holds only when $p \leq 3$. Moreover, we provide a counterexample to their result regarding $k$, thereby resolving the issue they raised. The paper concludes with an open problem. We demonstrate that, analogous to translation surfaces, the horizontal direction of this flow is either dense or periodic. Furthermore, we establish that the measure-theoretic and topological dynamics of the horocycle flow on dilation surfaces are equivalent. The proof relies on a version of Ratner's theorem applicable to the group of area-preserving affine transformations in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Finally, we examine the relationship between this work and recent findings by Zorich regarding the measure-theoretic properties of the geodesic flow. Specifically, we show that the time-$t$ map of the horocycle flow is measure-theoretically isomorphic to the time-$1/t$ map of the geodesic flow. Consequently, for a dilation surface where the horocycle flow is ergodic, the geodesic flow must also be ergodic. Conversely, if the horocycle flow is not ergodic, the geodesic flow is not ergodic; in this scenario, both flows possess a closed invariant cone field. These results hold for dilation surfaces whose linear part belongs to $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$. The paper concludes by discussing extensions to dilation surfaces with a broader class of linear transformations. distinct unitary representations of the Heisenberg group, each corresponding to a specific polarization. This paper extends those unitary representations to include "mixed" polarizations. We derive the explicit formulas for these "mixed" representations and validate them through unitary equivalence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these generalizations enable the reduction of coherent states for Heisenberg-Weyl groups that possess complex stabilizer subgroups. The study of these reduced states holds significant potential for applications in quantum information theory. Additionally, we examine the classical analogues of these reduced coherent states within both phase space and optical fibers. Finally, we explore a connection between coherent states and the orbit method. Specifically, we establish that the coadjoint orbit method can be extended to a broader class of Heisenberg-like groups, which includes certain Euclidean motion groups. This extension relies on constructing Kirillov-Kostant-Souriau symplectic forms on the duals of their Lie algebras. We also provide geometric interpretations of "mixed" polarizations using these symplectic forms. Leveraging this framework, we reduce the Hilbert space of irreducible representations for these Heisenberg-like groups and calculate their coherent states. Notably, the representations and coherent states for several Euclidean motion groups are derived as a direct consequence of this generalization. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the Hilbert spaces of irreducible representations of these groups and their coadjoint orbits. This correspondence yields unitary isomorphisms between the Hilbert spaces of irreducible representations of the Heisenberg-Weyl group and those of specific Euclidean motion groups. Consequently, the coherent states of these Euclidean motion groups are obtained directly from the coherent states of the Heisenberg-Weyl group. Finally, we apply these findings to quantum information theory, specifically in the context of stabilizer states. We show that all distinct stabilizer states can be generated via the coherent states of groups featuring complex stabilizer subgroups. This result offers a novel approach to constructing stabilizer states, distinct from the standard method using coherent states within irreducible representations of the Heisenberg-Weyl group. Moreover, we provide a geometric interpretation of various stabilizer states using coadjoint orbits of Euclidean motion groups. These results may prove valuable for quantum information processing involving interferometry and phase encoding. Additionally, we offer a geometric interpretation of the relationship between different stabilizer states. This work was partially conducted during a visit to the University of Ottawa. This paper introduces a novel approach allowing the server to perform classical computations of any complexity. The proposed method is based on a new classical reversible computing scheme where the client's computation is delegated to the server via Clifford circuits. Furthermore, the scheme is efficient, requiring the server to execute only a constant number of extra Clifford circuits. Finally, the approach is practical, utilizing a new method to generate Clifford circuits that ensures the client's computational cost remains independent of the size of the server's computation. This innovation enables the classical client to verify the server's computations with a cost that scales logarithmically with the size of the server's computation. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first proposal of a quantum verification scheme where the size of the client's computation scales logarithmically with the size of the server's computation. Additionally, the scheme is applicable to verifying the computation of reversible circuits. We demonstrate that, compared to the best existing scheme, our method reduces the classical client's computational cost by a factor of $O(N^2)$, where $N$ represents the number of qubits. This represents the most efficient quantum verification scheme to date. The paper also includes a detailed analysis of the scheme's security. Finally, we illustrate the scheme's practicality by applying it to verify the computation of a specific reversible circuit used in a quantum algorithm for solving the 3-SAT problem. In this application, the classical client's computation cost is independent of the number of variables in the 3-SAT problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantum verification scheme where the classical client's computational cost is independent of the problem size. The scheme is also applicable to verifying the computation of reversible circuits in other quantum algorithms. We believe this work holds great potential for practical applications. We conducted a survey of 100 English-language books to evaluate the quality of their corresponding accessible formats. Our findings indicate that while audio recordings are generally of high quality, they often omit essential non-textual elements like illustrations and footnotes, and suffer from pronunciation errors. Conversely, Braille translations frequently contain omissions and misinterpretations, particularly regarding formatting and specialized terms. These results underscore the urgent need for automated solutions to enhance the generation of accessible formats. To support this, we introduce a dataset comprising 1,000 sentences annotated with gold-standard labels for various Braille translation errors. This resource is intended to facilitate the development of machine learning models capable of producing more accurate translations. We conclude by outlining future directions for research in this field. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/brailletime/brailletime_dataset.

The research focuses on two specific systems: HD 140606, a binary with two massive stars, and HD 153318, which features a massive star paired with a less massive companion. To analyze these systems, we developed a numerical code that simulates the interaction between stellar winds and atmospheres. This code incorporates a parametric model for stellar winds and utilizes the 1D radiative transfer code MOOG to compute atmospheric properties. The resulting models are applied to the observed spectra of HD 140606 and HD 153318. Our findings indicate that the companion star in HD 140606 is experiencing wind ram pressure stripping, whereas the companion in HD 153318 is likely undergoing wind ram pressure ablation. Furthermore, we determined that the primary star in HD 140606 has a mass-loss rate of $1.1 \times 10^{-7} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, while the primary in HD 153318 loses mass at a rate of $1.5 \times 10^{-9} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. These findings suggest that the primary star in HD 153318 may be a stripped-envelope star, whereas the primary in HD 140606 appears to be a normal star. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these results for the future evolution of these close binary systems. This study employs a three-dimensional hydrodynamic model to examine the swimming dynamics of this organism. Additionally, the propulsion mechanism is analyzed by investigating the swimming behavior of a hypothetical entity composed of a spherical body with a single flagellum. By comparing the performance of *P. aeruginosa* with this simplified model, the study concludes that the bacterium's forward swimming speed is primarily determined by the flagellar bundle's CCW rotation. AC have identified a class of protoplanetary disks featuring a prominent inner gap, which are hypothesized to contain a forming planet. This study examines whether such a gap can be explained by a planet located at the gap's center. We conducted 2D hydrodynamical simulations of gas in Keplerian rotation, modeling dust transport via advection-diffusion. Our results indicate that a planet situated at the inner edge can create a significant annular gap, though the gap width is narrower than what is typically observed in ALMA data. Furthermore, the planet generates a secondary dust ring just outside the gap, a feature that aligns well with ALMA findings. However, the dust surface density within this ring is lower than observed in some ALMA disks, suggesting that additional mechanisms may be required to account for the higher densities. Additionally, we investigated the influence of turbulence on gas and dust distribution. While turbulent diffusion prevents the formation of a gap, it simultaneously raises the dust surface density in the region surrounding the planet. These findings offer a potential explanation for the low dust surface densities detected by ALMA in certain inner gaps. Finally, we explored the effects of varying the inner boundary conditions on disk structure. Our simulations demonstrate that the inner disk's structure is highly sensitive to these boundary conditions. In summary, our results suggest that a planet at the inner edge can account for the observed annular gaps and secondary rings in Kepler disks, while also addressing the discrepancies between modeled and observed dust surface densities. These insights may aid in interpreting future ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/leeyu123/PlanetGap. The objective is to determine the magnitude of this force required to initiate motion. The problem assumes that the maximum static frictional force is proportional to the disk's mass. Next, the problem considers the case where the largest disk is supported by the second largest disk. In this situation, the normal force acting on the largest disk is reduced to $N_{\text{applied}} = N_{\text{applied}} mg$. Therefore, the minimum force required to move the largest disk is $F_{\text{min}} = \mu N_{\text{applied}} mg$.

The problem then examines the case where the largest disk is supported by the third largest disk. Consequently, the minimum force required to move the largest disk is $F_{\text{min}} = \mu N_{\text{applied}} mg$.

Finally, the problem considers the general case where the largest disk is supported by the $k$-th largest disk. In this situation, the normal force acting on the largest disk is reduced to $N_{\text{applied}} = N_{\text{applied}} mg$. ### 1. Introduction
A taxonomy is a hierarchical classification system that organizes a set of documents or concepts into a tree-like structure. While taxonomies facilitate the organization of vast amounts of information, making them easier to navigate and understand, manually constructing them is time-consuming and costly. Consequently, there is a significant demand for methods that can automatically extract taxonomies from training data. This paper presents a method for multi-domain, multi-label classification that learns taxonomies from training data and applies them to unlabeled documents from new domains. The proposed method is assessed using two datasets: one focused on a single domain and another on multiple domains.

SciTaxo is a dataset designed for single-domain, multi-label classification, comprising scientific abstracts annotated with taxonomic labels. It includes three sub-datasets:

This study examines the viability of a WIMP scenario within a supersymmetric framework featuring a non-minimal $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry. We analyze the parameter space for neutralino WIMPs, incorporating both direct detection constraints from XENON1T and indirect detection limits derived from gamma-ray observations of dwarf galaxies and the galactic center. Furthermore, we explore the implications of recent observations of a 1.4 TeV gamma-ray line in the Milky Way's center, which may suggest dark matter annihilation into $\chi\bar{\chi} \to b\bar{b}$ or $\chi\bar{\chi} \to \gamma\gamma$. Our findings indicate that the observed gamma-ray spectrum can be replicated by neutralino WIMPs with masses of approximately 1.4 TeV, provided the $b$-quark annihilation channel is suppressed. This outcome is consistent with the model's predictions for the gamma-ray line originating from electron-positron annihilation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model remains compatible with indirect detection constraints from the Fermi-LAT observation of the Cygnus region. Finally, we show that the model can achieve thermal relic abundance through coannihilation mechanisms involving the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) and the second lightest supersymmetric particle (SLSP) within the early universe. These results suggest that the proposed model offers a viable explanation for dark matter. Keywords: Supersymmetry, Weakly Interacting Massive Particle, Non-minimal $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry. We demonstrate that for any compact subset $K \subset M$, the energy of $\phi_i$ on $K$ converges to the energy of $\phi_0$ as $i$ approaches infinity. This result extends a theorem by Schoen and Yau, which originally applied to minimal immersions. A significant application involves a sequence of stable, degree-one harmonic maps from $(M,g)$ to a compact target $(N,h)$; under these conditions, there exists a subsequence that converges smoothly to a minimal map. This finding generalizes work by Schoen and Yau and Li and Zhang, as it imposes no assumptions on the curvature of $(N,h)$. Furthermore, we establish a similar result for weakly harmonic maps from $(M,g)$ to a complete, non-compact target $(N,h)$ possessing non-negative sectional curvature. In this scenario, the existence of a degree-one harmonic map $\phi_0$ implies the same smooth convergence. This approach to stable harmonic maps offers an alternative to the theory developed by Chen and Fang. Additionally, we provide a counterexample illustrating that smooth convergence cannot be guaranteed if the non-negative curvature condition on $(N,h)$ is removed. Finally, we examine the case where $(N,h)$ is compact with non-positive curvature, proving that a bounded energy condition is sufficient to ensure smooth convergence. This finding aligns with established results for harmonic maps into manifolds with non-positive curvature. Finally, we present a counterexample showing that smooth convergence fails if the curvature condition on $(N,h)$ is relaxed to allow for a single point of zero curvature. This counterexample also applies to the case where $(N,h)$ is compact with non-positive curvature but contains exactly one point of zero curvature. These findings complement recent research by Li and Wang. The primary tools employed are the monotonicity formula and a gap phenomenon for the singular set of singular Ricci metrics. This approach is demonstrated using the most straightforward example: a one-dimensional flow featuring a single stagnation point. In this scenario, the steady-state probability density function (PDF) exhibits a power-law tail with an exponent determined by the sign of the stagnation region's vorticity. Furthermore, this framework can be extended to more complex scenarios, such as two-dimensional flows with a single stagnation point and three-dimensional flows with a single zero. We conclude by outlining the necessary generalizations for these examples to fully capture the non-Gaussian nature of the PDFs observed in the far tails of the Lagrangian PDFs. These findings may prove valuable for developing more accurate PDF-based models of geophysical turbulence. Additionally, the methodology may have broader applications in the design of stochastic processes for various purposes, including the generation of random numbers and the creation of new random processes. Specifically, we demonstrate that the azimuthal dependence of the hadronic tensor, characterized by the $A_T$ and $A_{LT}^{\perp}$ structure functions, can be derived from elastic scattering through a procedure known as "unfolding." is a critical challenge. This paper introduces a novel privacy-preserving location service that utilizes a new spatial clustering algorithm to group nearby users and generate a cloaked region. The system's core objective is to minimize the distance between the true location and the resulting cloaked area. To achieve this, the study proposes a new clustering method called the Minimum Distance Spatial Clustering (MDSC) algorithm. MDSC operates by first identifying the nearest neighbor for each user and then recursively grouping them into a cloaked region. The authors demonstrate that MDSC offers superior privacy protection compared to existing methods, such as DBSCAN, while maintaining comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, the paper presents a new algorithm, MDSC-N, which adapts MDSC for dynamic environments by incorporating a forgetting factor to handle moving users. Experimental results confirm that MDSC-N also provides enhanced privacy protection relative to other methods. Finally, the study evaluates the performance of both MDSC and MDSC-N within a simulated system. The findings indicate that the proposed approach reduces the average response time by 10.5% and 11.5% for MDSC and MDSC-N, respectively, compared to DBSCAN. Additionally, the average number of requests per cloaked region is reduced by 10.5% and 11.5% for MDSC and MDSC-N, respectively, when compared to the DBSCAN-based baseline. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in delivering improved privacy protection. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishek1234567890/mdsc.

This paper investigates the communication complexity of such networks, specifically focusing on transmitting a single bit. We demonstrate that a single bit can be successfully transmitted with a non-zero probability if and only if the network size does not exceed $2^{\mathcal{O}(\log^* n)}$, where $n$ represents the number of nodes and $\log^*$ denotes the iterated logarithm. This finding establishes a lower bound on communication complexity that surpasses previously known results by a factor of $\log n$. Furthermore, we present a randomized algorithm capable of transmitting a single bit from any configuration of $n$ nodes within $2^{\mathcal{O}(\log^* n)}$ time steps with high probability. This algorithm achieves an optimal trade-off between communication complexity and transmission time. Additionally, we provide a randomized algorithm that transmits a single bit from $n$ nodes in $2^{\mathcal{O}(\log^* n)}$ time steps using $\mathcal{O}(n)$ bits of communication with high probability. Finally, we introduce a deterministic algorithm for single-bit transmission from $n$ nodes in $2^{\mathcal{O}(\log^* n)}$ time steps with $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ bit communication, improving upon the prior best deterministic algorithm's $n^3$ bound. Our findings indicate that the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) is determined by the electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) and the logarithmic energy scale ($\omega_{\ln}$). Specifically, $\lambda$ is heavily influenced by the density of states at the Fermi level, while $\omega_{\ln}$ is governed by the phonon spectral function near the superconducting gap energy. We determined that $\lambda$ and $\omega_{\ln}$ reach their peak values at the hole-like Fermi surface, which is linked to the Ni $3d$ bands. Consequently, the superconducting gap is situated within the energy range of the Ni $3d$ bands. Finally, we calculated $T_c$ to be 2.5 K. These results align well with the experimentally observed $T_c$ of 2.4 K. Furthermore, we identified that the superconducting gap is anisotropic, exhibiting a significantly larger value in the $k_y$ direction compared to the $k_x$ direction. This anisotropy stems from the distinct phonon spectral functions along these axes, driven by the differing masses of La and Ni atoms. Ultimately, the superconductivity in LaNi$_2$Al$_{10}$ is attributed to the strong electron-phonon coupling associated with the hole-like Fermi surface. These insights are expected to be applicable to other rare-earth transition metal aluminides. This study examines the superconducting state within the FeSe$_{1-x}$Se$_x$ system, which exhibits Se-induced nematic fluctuations. By employing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and specific heat measurements, we investigated the evolution of the superconducting gap across the entire doping range. Our findings reveal that the superconducting gap is nodeless in the Se-deficient regime but develops nodes as doping increases. Furthermore, we observed that the specific heat shows no anomaly at the Se-doping-induced nematic quantum critical point (QCP). These results indicate that the superconducting state in FeSe$_{1-x}$Se$_x$ is driven by Se-doping-enhanced nematic fluctuations, rather than by the Se-doping QCP itself. Additionally, the specific heat data suggest that the superconducting gap is predominantly anisotropic. Collectively, these observations support a scenario where the superconducting state arises from the competition between Se-doping-enhanced nematic fluctuations and strong spin fluctuations. This proposed mechanism offers a potential pathway for achieving high-temperature superconductivity in FeSe-based materials. These findings are consistent with prior theoretical predictions. We examine the remaining parameter space after applying all current experimental limits, including those derived from the recently observed diphoton excess. Our analysis integrates a wide array of theoretical and experimental restrictions, such as perturbative unitarity, vacuum stability, and diverse flavor, electroweak, and Higgs constraints. We provide detailed discussions on the implications of various diphoton signal strengths and their impact on the allowed regions. Furthermore, we explore the potential of future lepton colliders in probing the parameter space of the Type-II 2HDM. Finally, we outline the prospects for discovering additional Higgs bosons at the CEPC and FCC-ee. This study serves as a foundational reference for upcoming experimental searches for extra Higgs bosons at high-energy colliders. Additionally, the methodology employed can be readily extended to other Standard Model extensions. The complete analysis is available in machine-readable format at \url{http://www.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/2hdm/}. We also present a user-friendly interface for this tool at \url{http://www.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/2hdm/}. This interface allows users to visualize the parameter space for different signal strengths and theoretical assumptions, and to access the machine-readable files. We anticipate that this tool will serve as a valuable resource for the physics community. Furthermore, we have included a discussion on the impact of including the current ATLAS diphoton search results, which were not yet finalized at the time of our initial analysis. We conclude that the overall picture remains unchanged. Finally, we address the issue of the diphoton signal's dependence on the heavy Higgs boson mass $m_H$. We demonstrate that the allowed parameter space is largely independent of $m_H$ for masses exceeding 600 GeV. This finding is supported by a detailed examination of the 750 GeV resonance. We also discuss the implications of the recent ATLAS search for a 750 GeV resonance in the diphoton channel. We show that the observed signal can be accommodated by the 2HDM, though it is not the only viable explanation. We emphasize the need for further analysis to clarify the nature of this signal. offers a compelling explanation for the Baryon Asymmetry of the Universe (BAU) by utilizing the decay of $B$ mesons. This scenario relies on the violation of both $CP$ and $FL$ symmetries, which are inherent in the Standard Model. However, the resulting BAU is too small to account for the observed universe, necessitating new physics. We investigate the impact of a new $Z'$ gauge boson on $B$ meson decays, specifically within the $Z'$ model that successfully resolves the $R_{D^{(*)}}$ anomaly. Our analysis reveals that this new $Z'$ gauge boson induces significant modifications in both the rate and the BAU. Furthermore, we examine the constraints imposed by $B$ meson decays and the resulting BAU, demonstrating that these effects can be enhanced by introducing an additional new $Z'$ gauge boson. This additional boson also influences the mixing of the $Z'$ model, thereby affecting the BAU. We conclude that the BAU can be amplified by incorporating an extra $Z'$ gauge boson, and we provide specific examples to illustrate this enhancement. Additionally, we analyze the constraints arising from $B$ meson decays and the generated BAU, showing that these constraints can be strengthened by the presence of an extra $Z'$ gauge boson. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting this new $Z'$ gauge boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our findings indicate that the LHC can identify this new $Z'$ gauge boson through the decay of $Z'$ into $t\bar{t}$, with an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$. This detection is feasible when the mass of the $Z'$ boson exceeds 1 TeV. These results underscore the effectiveness of the $Z'$ model in generating the BAU and its potential for experimental verification at the LHC. In summary, the $Z'$ model can produce the BAU via $B$ meson decays, and this process can be observed at the LHC. The $t\bar{t}$ decay channel of the $Z'$ boson offers a viable pathway for detecting the new $Z'$ gauge boson. **1. Introduction**

Variational inference (VI) is a widely adopted technique for approximating the intractable posterior distribution in Bayesian inference. VI formulates posterior approximation as an optimization problem, aiming to identify the distribution that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the true posterior. However, directly minimizing this KL divergence is typically intractable. Consequently, VI employs an upper bound on this divergence to enable optimization. This work focuses on enhancing the bound used in VI to better approximate the true posterior.

The standard VI approach employs the Kullback-Leibler divergence as a measure of dissimilarity between two probability distributions. The objective is to find the distribution that minimizes the divergence from the true posterior. Since direct minimization is intractable, a lower bound is employed instead. This lower bound consists of two components: the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and the KL divergence between the true and approximate posteriors. The ELBO is optimized to maximize the bound, while the KL divergence is minimized to reduce the discrepancy between the true and approximate posteriors.

This phenomenon is driven by the coupling between the spin system's internal degrees of freedom and the lattice's orbital space. Specifically, the spin-orbit interaction induces an effective anisotropy within the Hamiltonian, which stabilizes chiral spin liquids. Furthermore, we establish that every morphism between ordered blueprints corresponds to a ring homomorphism, and we provide a characterization of ideal congruences within the context of ordered blueprints. These findings offer an alternative perspective on rings and offer significant utility for algebraic geometry over ordered blueprints. This theory offers a natural setting for algebraic geometry over ordered blueprints, enabling the study of algebraic varieties equipped with an ordering on their coordinate rings. of minimal qualified sets. This paper introduces a novel method for constructing secret sharing schemes based on specific graph classes, with a focus on planar graphs. Our approach utilizes graph contractions to generate new schemes from existing ones, ensuring that the resulting set of minimal qualified sets forms a simplicial complex. This technique enables the application of various graph-theoretic tools to analyze the characteristics of the plans produced. We derive upper bounds on the number of minimal qualified sets for schemes generated from planar graphs and demonstrate the practicality of these bounds by presenting several illustrative examples. Furthermore, we extend our findings to schemes derived from graphs with restricted edge crossings. To our knowledge, this work offers the first bounds on the number of minimal qualified sets in secret sharing schemes derived from planar graphs. Additionally, we establish upper bounds for schemes derived from graphs with at most $k$ edge crossings, specifically for $k=2$ and $k=3$. Finally, we propose an open problem concerning secret sharing schemes derived from planar 3-connected graphs. This problem seeks to determine the tightest possible upper bound on the number of minimal qualified sets for such schemes. Solving this problem would provide a tight upper bound for schemes derived from planar cubic graphs, a class of graphs that has garnered significant interest recently. This interest stems from their application in designing secret sharing schemes for sensor networks. A key objective in this context is to minimize the number of shares required to reconstruct a secret, a goal directly addressed by the bounds discussed in this paper. By providing tight upper bounds on the number of shares needed to reconstruct a secret from a planar graph-based scheme, this work contributes to the broader effort to optimize sensor network designs. This contribution is particularly relevant given the recent focus on using graph-theoretic methods to achieve efficient sensor network designs. Additionally, the problem of determining tight upper bounds for secret sharing schemes derived from planar 3-connected graphs is relevant to the study of Schnyder woods. Schnyder woods are a specific type of graph embedding that has been extensively researched for their applications in graph drawing and other areas. The connection between Schnyder woods and secret sharing schemes highlights the interdisciplinary nature of this research and its potential impact on both graph theory and practical applications. In conclusion, this paper offers new insights and tools for understanding and optimizing secret sharing schemes, with a particular emphasis on those derived from planar graphs and graphs with limited edge crossings. The bounds presented in this work provide a foundation for future research and applications in these areas. Overall, this research advances the field

solitons (PTS) have been observed in the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) across diverse physical systems, including Bose-Einstein condensates, optical lattices, and photonic structures. This study demonstrates that the NLSE governing PTS can be derived from a discrete system of coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) featuring local nonlinear coupling. By employing a multiple scales method, we analyze the slow dynamics of these solitons, revealing that their behavior is governed by a local nonlinearity parameter. This finding indicates that the NLSE serves as an effective continuum model for PTS dynamics, contingent upon the specific nature of the nonlinear coupling. Furthermore, the identified constraint on nonlinear coupling suggests a viable pathway for constructing effective continuum models for solitons in other discrete systems. Finally, we illustrate the validity of this continuum model by examining the dynamics of a pair of coherently coupled PTS within a local nonlinearly coupled network. The observed dynamics align with the continuum model predictions, confirming the model's accuracy. These results offer a straightforward approach for modeling soliton dynamics in discrete systems where nonlinear coupling is inherently local. Additionally, the continuum framework presented here can be extended to model PTS dynamics in higher-dimensional systems. In homogeneous networks, the model predicts a transition from asynchronous to synchronous states as coupling strength increases, a shift driven by a bifurcation within the mean-field equations. Conversely, in heterogeneous networks, the transition from asynchronous to synchronous dynamics is governed by the distribution of neuronal parameters. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of the corresponding stochastic partial differential equation. Furthermore, the research explores the impact of time delays in coupling, revealing that they induce a variety of novel patterns in synchronous networks, including oscillations, traveling waves, and mixed modes. The delayed mean-field equations were solved using both finite difference and spectral methods. Ultimately, this work underscores the effectiveness of the mean-field approximation in describing and forecasting the behavior of large theta neuronal networks. These insights may also apply to other neuronal models, such as the leaky integrate-and-fire model, which also exhibit a transition to synchronous activity via a bifurcation in their mean-field formulations. This capability is particularly valuable for analyzing and predicting the dynamics of extensive neuronal networks. Finally, the study examines the implications of these results for neural circuits within the brain. Neural circuits are extensively distributed throughout the brain, and their synchronization is linked to various neurological disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and autism. Consequently, the proposed mean-field approach offers a means to investigate the dynamics of neural circuits associated with these conditions. Additionally, the methodology can be extended to analyze the impact of neural circuit damage on brain function. Neural circuits are integral to numerous brain activities, including motor control, memory formation, and sensory processing. By applying the mean-field approach, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how these circuits contribute to overall brain function. Ultimately, this understanding may facilitate the development of more effective treatments for neurological disorders. In summary, this work provides a robust framework for analyzing and predicting the behavior of large theta neuronal networks, with broad applications ranging from neuroscience to the study of neural circuit dysfunction. a one-dimensional lattice where particles interact with a time-dependent electric field. The model incorporates both charge and spin degrees of freedom, featuring a single orbital per site. The spin component is governed by an on-site anisotropic Heisenberg Hamiltonian, while the orbital degree of freedom is described by a charge Hamiltonian that includes hopping, a charge anisotropy term, and a time-varying electric field. We analyze how the spin and charge anisotropy parameters, alongside the electric field's amplitude and frequency, influence the system's behavior. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which the model exhibits a spin-charge separation regime. Finally, we compare our findings with previous studies on this and related models. This research represents a significant step toward comprehending the intricate dynamics of interacting quantum systems subjected to external driving forces. The methodologies employed here can be extended to investigate more complex systems, such as those with multiple orbitals per site, frustrated lattices, and those exhibiting strong correlations. These extensions are crucial for understanding the behavior of strongly correlated systems found in various condensed matter contexts, including Mott insulators, high-temperature superconductors, and quantum spin liquids. Additionally, the study's results may prove relevant to other fields involving interacting quantum systems under external driving, such as cold atom systems and quantum information processing. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles governing the behavior of interacting quantum systems subjected to external driving forces. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the model and outlines the theoretical framework; Section 3 presents the results and discusses their implications; and Section 4 provides a summary and conclusions. In Section 2, we define the model and establish the theoretical framework. We begin by specifying the lattice geometry and the nature of the interactions between particles and the electric field. We then formulate the Hamiltonian governing the system's behavior, which includes terms for particle hopping, on-site interactions, and the time-dependent electric field. We also specify the initial conditions for the system and describe the methods used to calculate observable quantities, such as occupation numbers and correlation functions. In Section 3, we present the results of our numerical simulations, which examine how the system's behavior changes in response to variations in the electric field's amplitude and frequency, as well as the on-site interactions. We analyze how these factors influence the system's dynamics and discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of interacting quantum systems. We also explore the possibility of a spin-charge separation regime and discuss the conditions under which this occurs.

a novel, non-invasive method for quantifying the severity of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) using a single-channel electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded during sleep.

**Background:** OSA is a prevalent sleep disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep, leading to intermittent breathing cessation. It is strongly linked to cardiovascular conditions, including hypertension, heart failure, and stroke. While polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard for OSA diagnosis, it is costly and requires specialized equipment and expertise. Consequently, there is a significant demand for alternative diagnostic approaches that are more accessible and affordable.

**Methodology:** The research utilizes a dataset comprising 1,000 ECG segments, each lasting 30 seconds, sourced from the Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS). These segments were manually annotated by experts as either OSA-positive or negative. Feature extraction involved calculating time-domain, frequency-domain, and time-frequency features, followed by feature selection using a correlation-based filter method. Classification was performed using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm.

**Results:** The study achieved an accuracy of 80.2%, a sensitivity of 78.8%, and a specificity of 81.6%.

**Conclusion:** The findings indicate that ECG signals can effectively predict OSA severity. This suggests that ECG-based methods offer a viable alternative for OSA assessment, providing a less resource-intensive option compared to traditional PSG.

**Keywords:** Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), Sleep Apnea Severity, Correlation-based Feature Selection, Electrocardiogram (ECG), Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS), Support Vector Machine (SVM).

We say that $f$ and $g$ are orthogonally subordinate if, for every $z$ in the upper half-plane, the images $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are orthogonal. This note establishes a characterization of these functions based on the properties of $f$ and a specific function $h$ defined by the relation $f \circ g = h$. Specifically, $h$ must be a self-map of the upper half-plane that fixes the point at infinity and possesses a non-zero derivative at that point. Furthermore, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for orthogonally subordinate functions to be holomorphic. As an application, we offer a characterization of holomorphic functions with non-vanishing derivatives in terms of holomorphic mappings $f$ and $g$ such that $f \circ g$ equals that derivative. Additionally, we present a characterization of holomorphic functions $f$ satisfying $f'(z) \neq 0$ for all $z$ in the upper half-plane, based on the conditions imposed on $f$ and a holomorphic function $u$ where $u \circ f = u - 1$. Finally, we demonstrate that if $u$ is a holomorphic function with a non-vanishing derivative, then $u$ is linear if and only if there exists a holomorphic function $v$ such that $u \circ v = u - 1$. These findings are derived from a more general result concerning holomorphic functions $u$ possessing a non-zero derivative at the point at infinity within the upper half-plane. Our results extend a previous theorem by the second author, which characterized holomorphic functions with non-vanishing derivatives in the unit disk. We propose a truthful mechanism that achieves an approximation ratio of $O(\log k)$, improving upon the best prior result of $O(k^{1/3})$. Our approach begins by demonstrating that any optimal allocation can be realized using at most $O(k)$ buyers. Leveraging this finding, we design a mechanism that allocates items to the $O(k)$ buyers with the highest valuations. We establish that the expected welfare generated by this mechanism is within an $O(\log k)$ factor of the optimal welfare. Furthermore, we show that this allocation can be implemented through a direct mechanism with an expected welfare loss of no more than a constant factor. Finally, we extend these results to settings with additive valuations and independent valuations, and we address the case where buyer identities are unknown. In all scenarios, our mechanism yields an $O(\log k)$ approximation, surpassing the previous best approximation of $O(k^{1/3})$. Additionally, we examine a related problem involving selling $k$ items to $n$ buyers with $k$-submodular valuations. We present a truthful mechanism achieving an $O(\sqrt{k})$ approximation, outperforming the prior best ratio of $O(k^{2/3})$. Our method involves a two-step process: first, identifying a subset of buyers to invite to a second round, and second, selling the items to these invited buyers. We prove that the expected welfare of this mechanism is within an $O(\sqrt{k})$ factor of the optimal welfare. We also demonstrate that this allocation can be realized by a direct mechanism with an expected welfare loss of at most a constant factor. We further show that the expected welfare loss is bounded by $O(\sqrt{k})$ even when buyer identities are unknown. To our knowledge, this is the first mechanism to achieve an $O(\sqrt{k})$ approximation for this problem. Our results are complemented by lower bounds on the possible approximation ratio. We investigate how the initial conditions influence the final event characteristics and the development of event-by-event fluctuations. Our results indicate that the final observables are largely independent of the chosen initial conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the event-by-event fluctuations observed in the final stages can be effectively reproduced by the transport model, provided that the fluctuations in the intermediate phases are accurately represented. These findings suggest that the final observables can serve as a sensitive probe for the intermediate-state dynamics. Additionally, we find that the variance of the net-proton multiplicity distribution in central events at 14.5 AGeV is significantly lower than that in nucleon-nucleon collisions at the same energy. This study examines the impact of communication latency on the execution time of PEAs. By analyzing the time complexity of a representative parallel genetic algorithm, we identified bottlenecks caused by communication latency. To address this, we introduced a computational model that incorporates such latency. Our findings indicate that the introduction of communication latency can significantly alter the execution time of PEAs. **1. Introduction**

Formal verification has been shown to enhance software quality and reliability, making it a critical tool for safety-critical software development. Nevertheless, the high cost and time investment required for this process often deter practitioners from adopting it. To address this, we present a technique to expedite formal proof development through the utilization of machine learning.

Our technique employs a neural network to predict the result of each proof step, subsequently guiding the proof search. We implemented this approach using a ProverVerif-based neural network that learns from proofs within the Coq proof assistant. Our results indicate that this method can significantly reduce the time needed to construct proofs. We successfully applied the technique to prove 100 safety-critical theorems, realizing an average performance gain of 20 times over human developers and 30 times over the use of ProverVerif without guidance. Additionally, the technique exhibits excellent generalization, enabling the reuse of knowledge across different domains such as system design, data structures, and algorithms.

Formal verification entails the mathematical proof of a system's correctness. This process typically includes two primary components: a logical framework and a proof assistant. The logical framework defines the rules for constructing proofs, while the proof assistant provides the tools to execute them.

of lipid bilayers have sparked significant debate. This study addresses the issue by examining how cholesterol influences the area-dilation modulus ($K_A$) through molecular dynamics simulations of pure DPPC bilayers with varying cholesterol concentrations. We employed the CHARMM36 and Slipid force fields, which are currently the most prevalent models for lipid simulations. Our results indicate that both force fields predict a rise in $K_A$ as cholesterol concentration increases. Specifically, the Slipid force field demonstrates a steeper increase in $K_A$ compared to CHARMM36. Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between $K_A$ and the order parameter, revealing that the order parameter alone cannot account for the variations in $K_A$ across different cholesterol levels. Finally, we investigated the role of lipid tail ordering in modulating $K_A$ by analyzing the radial distribution functions of tail carbon atoms. These findings suggest that the enhanced tail ordering induced by cholesterol contributes to the observed increase in $K_A$. Our results align with experimental data, although the absolute values derived from the force fields differ from experimental measurements. Additionally, we observed that the order parameter increases with cholesterol concentration up to 50%, after which it remains constant. This saturation effect is attributed to the formation of a liquid-ordered phase at higher cholesterol concentrations. Finally, we evaluated the impact of the water model on the calculated $K_A$ values. Our analysis indicates that the standard TIP3P water model yields $K_A$ values that are approximately 20% lower than those produced by the Slipid-TIP4P/2005 water model. These outcomes are consistent with prior studies on DPPC bilayers. Overall, our findings indicate that the specific water model utilized in simulations can significantly affect the calculated $K_A$ values. This work underscores the necessity of utilizing realistic force fields and water models to achieve accurate representations of lipid bilayer properties. Ultimately, this study provides valuable insights into the complex interactions between cholesterol and lipid bilayers. traditionally focused on planets orbiting single stars, the growing number of exoplanets in multiple star systems suggests that planet formation and evolution are influenced by the presence of companions. This project aims to quantify the impact of stellar multiplicity on the exoplanet population. To achieve this, we examine the orbital and physical characteristics of exoplanets within systems containing more than one star, comparing them to those in single-star systems. Our findings indicate that the fundamental properties of exoplanets, including their masses and orbital periods, are statistically indistinguishable between single and multiple star systems. However, we observe a significantly higher frequency of giant planets in wide circumstellar orbits (periods exceeding 10 years) within multiple star systems. This suggests that stellar companions may facilitate the formation of massive planets in distant orbits, potentially by enabling the accretion of material from the protoplanetary disk's outer regions. Furthermore, we identify a notable absence of planets with orbital periods greater than 10 years in multiple star systems, implying that stellar companions may destabilize planets in wide orbits. These results highlight the critical role of stellar multiplicity in shaping the exoplanet population and offer valuable constraints for planet formation and evolution models. $G$ where two players, Alice and Bob, take turns selecting vertices. Alice begins by picking a vertex $v$, after which Bob chooses a neighbor. The game concludes when a player cannot make a valid move; Alice wins if Bob is unable to select a neighbor, while Bob wins if Alice cannot pick an initial vertex. Alice employs a strategy to maximize the length of the game, whereas Bob uses a strategy to minimize it. The primary objective is to analyze the outcomes of these optimal strategies for both players.

The authors establish that Bob possesses a winning strategy for $G$ if and only if $G$ contains an induced subgraph $H$ that is either an odd cycle or an odd cycle with chords, where the length of $H$ is at most 7. Furthermore, Alice wins if and only if $G$ has an induced odd cycle or odd cycle with chords of length at most 5. Additionally, the study proves that for any graph $G$ with a perfect matching, Bob can guarantee a win by selecting a vertex from a matching edge such that he can pair every edge in $G$ with a path of length at most 2, with each vertex used exactly once.

Finally, the paper presents a game-theoretic characterization of $k$-choosable graphs. Specifically, for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, the authors demonstrate that Alice and Bob have winning strategies for the game on $G$ if and only if $G$ is $k$-choosable, provided that $n$ and $m$ satisfy certain conditions. This result offers a novel approach to determining the choosability of graphs. As a specific application, the authors determine the winning strategies for Alice and Bob when $G$ is a complete bipartite graph.

Keywords: $k$-choosable graph; game on a graph; complete bipartite graph; perfect matching.

To achieve precise and efficient static analysis, this domain must be sufficiently rich to model program properties accurately and sufficiently compact to support a small number of operations. This paper introduces a novel abstract domain for control flow analysis, built upon the concept of control flow summaries. These summaries are derived from a program's source code or control flow graph and are combined using a specific control flow operator. We demonstrate that this domain is both sound and terminating for first-order programs with recursive functions, and we outline strategies to enhance its precision. We validate its effectiveness through experimental results on real-world Java programs. This approach is integrated into the overall framework and evaluated empirically. This study examines the magnetic properties of the half-metallic compound Sr$_2$CrMoO$_6$ using density functional theory. Our analysis reveals that the half-metallic nature of this material is closely tied to the specific electronic configuration of the Cr$^{3+}$ ion. Furthermore, we find that the magnetic behavior is governed by the interplay between the narrow $d_{yz}$ and $d_{zx}$ orbitals of the Cr$^{3+}$ ion and the broader $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ orbital of the Mo$^{5+}$ ion. These findings offer a deeper understanding of the magnetic mechanisms in Sr$_2$CrMoO$_6$ and may also provide insights into other perovskite systems. Additionally, we explore the impact of various external perturbations on the material's half-metallic character. Our results indicate that applying pressure can induce a transition from an antiferromagnetic half-metallic state to a ferromagnetic metallic state. Finally, we demonstrate that substituting Sr$_2$CrMoO$_6$ with Sr$_2$VO$_2$MoO$_6$ or Sr$_2$VO$_3$MoO$_6$ alters the magnetic ordering from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic. These outcomes offer valuable perspectives for future research on half-metallic oxides. **1. Introduction**

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant success in learning policies for various robotic tasks within continuous state-action spaces. However, the high sample complexity associated with many RL algorithms remains a major barrier to their practical application. Moreover, the black-box nature of these policies limits their interpretability, making it difficult to understand the rationale behind specific actions. This work addresses these issues by developing a structured representation of the RL policy. By modeling the policy as a Barycentric RNN, we ensure that the policy exhibits a convex relationship with the input state. This approach yields policies that are both sample-efficient and interpretable, as they can be characterized as a mixture of linear functions. The following sections detail the methodology and present experimental validation.

While their origin remains debated, the most widely accepted model attributes them to the precession of the inner accretion disc. This study examines the 2011 outburst of the type-C QPO source MAXI J1535-571, utilizing data from the Swift-BAT, NICER, and ISS instruments. We analyzed the evolution of the fractional amplitude of the precession frequency ($f_{\rm prec}$) and the fractional amplitude of the 2-10 keV disc component ($f_{\rm disc}$) throughout the outburst. Our results indicate that the correlation between $f_{\rm prec}$ and $f_{\rm disc}$ is not constant but evolves during the outburst. Furthermore, we observed a strong anti-correlation between $f_{\rm prec}$ and the fractional amplitude of the hard component ($f_{\rm hard}$), as well as between $f_{\rm disc}$ and $f_{\rm hard}$. These findings suggest that the disc's physical properties, such as its thickness, vary during the outburst. We also investigated the relationship between the precession frequency and the black hole spin, finding that the spin of MAXI J1535-571 likely decreased during the outburst. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the precession model. The observed evolution of the disc's physical properties and black hole spin may be explained by the interaction between the accretion disc and the corona. The analysis covers a broad spectrum of nonlinearity types, including subcritical, critical, and supercritical regimes, as well as cases with or without gradient terms. Specifically, we examine nonlinearities of the form $ f(u) = |u|^\ast u + g(u) $, where $ g $ satisfies a Lipschitz condition. The primary innovation lies in a refined iteration technique that generates Hölder continuous solutions with optimal Hölder exponents. This approach is subsequently applied to investigate the asymptotic behavior of solutions to the critical mean field equation $ \Delta u + \frac{8\pi e^{u}}{|x|^{\alpha}(\alpha + |x|^{\alpha})} = 0 $ defined on $ \mathbb{R}^N $ for $ N \geq 2 $ and $ \alpha \geq 0 $. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any radially symmetric, nonnegative solution $ u $ exhibits an asymptotic profile characterized by an optimal Hölder exponent. This result extends and improves upon the findings of Chanillo and Lin (1990) regarding the case $ \alpha = 0 $. Additionally, we present a novel, streamlined proof of Chanillo and Lin's result as a direct consequence of our work. Finally, we derive an alternative proof of Chanillo and Lin's result for the specific scenario where $ u $ possesses a finite limit at the origin. This particular outcome was previously established by Liang and Wei (2010) using a distinct methodology. Our proof diverges from theirs by leveraging the optimal Hölder regularity of weak solutions to semilinear elliptic equations on Lipschitz domains, a property established in our earlier research (Chen and Liang, 2019). We also provide a comprehensive overview of the relevant literature concerning this regularity property. Finally, we outline a generalization of Chanillo and Lin's result to a broader class of nonlinearities, demonstrating that solutions to $ \Delta u + \frac{8\pi e^{u}}{|x|^{\alpha}(\alpha + |x|^{\alpha})} = g(u) $ in $ \mathbb{R}^N $ share the same asymptotic behavior, provided $ g $ is a Lipschitz continuous function. This study examines the transport of a particle within a potential featuring two minima, where the system evolves under an external electric field. We analyze the time-dependent current fluctuations, known as dynamical currents, and demonstrate that their time-averaged value aligns with the time-dependent displacement. Furthermore, we identify a regime where dynamical current fluctuations exhibit negative values. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations. Our results offer valuable insights into the behavior of nanoscale objects, such as quantum dots, where the charge exhibits temporal fluctuations. Additionally, our findings may have implications for the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems. We also explore the relationship between the charge of an isolated object and the charge current it generates, revealing that the charge of the object is not conserved due to the emission of dynamical currents. Finally, we propose a method to calculate the entropy production of the system through these emitted currents. We conclude that the total entropy production, encompassing both the system and its environment, remains positive, thereby upholding the second law of thermodynamics. Bayesian approach to inverse problems, which typically involves a forward model and prior distributions for unknown parameters. In contrast, neural Bayesian inversion models the inverse problem directly as a mapping from data to unknowns, bypassing the explicit need for a forward model or prior distributions. This paper investigates the conditions required for neural Bayesian inversion to remain consistent with classical Bayes' rule. We demonstrate that neural Bayesian inversion can be interpreted as a novel nonparametric density estimation technique. Furthermore, we establish that neural Bayesian inversion is equivalent to a specific type of neural variational inference, where the variational density is represented by a neural network. Finally, we show that neural Bayesian inversion is mathematically equivalent to a specific neural network density estimation method, which we term neural Bayesian flow. This name reflects the method's core principle: the neural network is trained to reverse the data generation process, thereby flowing backward from data to unknowns. We validate the efficacy of neural Bayesian flow through a numerical experiment involving the inversion of a linear forward model. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyingyi/Neural-Bayesian-Flow-Inversion.

Keywords: Neural Bayesian inversion, Neural variational inference, Neural density estimation, Neural flow.

This challenge is particularly evident in distributed model predictive control (DMPC) for nonlinear systems, where the need to solve non-convex optimization problems at every time step often necessitates iterative algorithms. These iterations typically demand extensive information exchange, which can be costly in terms of bandwidth and computational resources. To address this, we propose a method that limits information exchange to a single data point per iteration. Specifically, we utilize a one-shot approach that transmits only the final solution of each iteration. We demonstrate that this strategy enables the system to converge to a solution that is arbitrarily close to optimal, provided a sufficient number of iterations are performed. Furthermore, we apply this concept to a distributed MPC framework for nonlinear systems, proving that the resulting closed-loop system achieves asymptotic stability and attains any desired level of performance. Finally, we illustrate the approach's effectiveness through a simulation of a distributed MPC scheme applied to a multi-agent system. The results show that the one-shot method achieves performance comparable to that of an iterative algorithm while requiring significantly less communication. Additionally, we observe that the one-shot approach outperforms non-iterative one-step MPC methods. These findings suggest that the proposed one-shot distributed MPC strategy is well-suited for applications where communication is expensive or bandwidth is limited. less" dark matter model proposed by Bertone et al. (2010), which posits that dark matter consists of heavy, self-interacting particles. We demonstrate that the model's viability is restricted to a narrow parameter range, specifically $10^{10} \lesssim m_{\rm DM} \lesssim 10^{11}$ GeV and $\sigma_{\rm DM} n_{\rm DM} \sim 1$ cm$^2$/s, where $m_{\rm DM}$ represents the particle mass and $\sigma_{\rm DM}$ the self-interaction cross-section. Our analysis reveals that the primary constraint arises from the inability of such particles to form the observed number of galaxies. We examine this constraint using a simple formation model and further validate it through N-body simulations. Additionally, we assess other significant constraints, including those from Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, galactic rotation curves, and the cosmic microwave background. Finally, we explore the connection between this scenario and the recently proposed "dark sector" framework. We conclude that the model remains viable only if dark matter interacts with a light partner particle via a long-range force. This interaction must be sufficiently strong to facilitate the formation of galaxies, yet weak enough to allow them to form within the observed timeframe. Consequently, the model's parameter space is confined to a very narrow region. Furthermore, we show that the model can be compatible with the observed abundance of galaxies if it is embedded within a broader "dark sector" containing additional particles. In this context, the dark sector's internal interactions can account for the necessary dark matter self-interactions. This suggests that the "dispersionless" model may serve as a viable alternative to cold dark matter. However, this interpretation necessitates the existence of a dark sector, which would also explain the absence of light particles beyond the Standard Model. Finally, we highlight that the dark sector scenario offers a natural resolution to the long-standing issue of the missing satellite problem. This paper introduces a new class of games featuring a global system utility that is a sum of convex functions of the agents' strategies. We propose a distributed algorithm enabling agents to reach the system's Nash equilibrium using only local data. We demonstrate that the algorithm's convergence guarantees depend on the properties of the global utility function, specifically its convexity and the smoothness of its gradient. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a multi-agent system engaged in a distributed model predictive control task. In this scenario, each agent optimizes its own cost function, which depends on both local and neighboring states, with the goal of driving the system to an equilibrium that minimizes the sum of these cost functions. Finally, we present simulation results confirming the algorithm's effectiveness. These findings are applicable to various scenarios, such as multi-agent motion planning, formation control, and multi-agent optimization. Additionally, this approach can be utilized to analyze the stability of large-scale interconnected systems. To our knowledge, this is the first work to address the stability analysis of such systems through the lens of Nash equilibrium. Our results indicate that, under specific conditions, the system state will converge to an equilibrium point. Although recent advancements have demonstrated that deep networks can surpass traditional methods, current architectures are often computationally intensive and memory-heavy. To address this, we propose applying network quantization to reduce both computational and memory costs. However, directly applying quantization to existing models yields suboptimal results.
